new_value: The B.W. Cooper public housing development, built between 1939 and 1941 and always called the Calliope, raised two generations of New Orleans musicians. The Neville brothers, pianist Willie Tee, the Dixie Cups and Henry Butler all lived here. Percy Miller, known as Master P, was raised in the Calliope by his grandparents, started No Limit Records in California, and moved the label to New Orleans around 1995. With his brothers C-Murder and Silkk the Shocker he made the project's name familiar to rap listeners nationwide, and No Limit sold more than fifty million albums by 2001. The complex flooded in 2005 and had been demolished by 2014, except for three brick buildings.
reason: Louisiana Landmarks Society (2020) records three original brick buildings still standing six years after the 2014 demolitions, so "fully demolished" is wrong; 2014 stands as year_end.

new_value: The H&R Bar, at the Central City corner of Second and Dryades streets, was the headquarters of the Wild Magnolias. Its hand-painted sign gave 1966 as the year it was established, two years after Bo Dollis became the gang's Big Chief. On Sunday evenings in the months before Carnival the Indians held practice inside, drumming and chanting. Dollis's voice caught the ear of Quint Davis, then a college student, which led to the 1970 single "Handa Wanda," recorded in Baton Rouge with Willie Tee on keyboards and Snooks Eaglin on guitar behind the chant. Monk Boudreaux's Golden Eagles recorded the live album Lightning and Thunder in the bar in 1988. Fire destroyed it in 2001; the lot is empty.
reason: WWOZ states the single was recorded in Baton Rouge; saying so removes any implication that it was recorded in the bar.

new_value: Mahalia Jackson, born in 1911 a few blocks away in the uptown riverside neighborhood now called the Black Pearl, learned to sing in this church. Her grandfather, Paul Clark, preached here from the 1910s. She stood out in the youth choir, moved up to the adult choir, and was baptized in the river as a member at fourteen, about 1925. The congregation's "Dr. Watts" hymn singing and its foot-tapping, hand-clapping bounce shaped her style before she left for Chicago as a teenager. In 1956 she arranged a live national television broadcast of a Christmas service from the church, and her funeral procession passed it in 1972. The congregation still worships here.

new_value: In 1956 Cosimo Matassa moved out of his J&M studio on North Rampart Street into a former warehouse on Governor Nicholls Street in the lower French Quarter, and renamed the business with what everyone already called it. Here a core of session players, among them saxophonists Lee Allen and Red Tyler, backed Fats Domino on "I'm Walkin'" and Little Richard on "Lucille." Huey "Piano" Smith's hits, Frankie Ford's "Sea Cruise," and Allen Toussaint's early productions followed, including Ernie K-Doe's "Mother-in-Law" and Chris Kenner's "I Like It Like That" in 1961. By 1967 Matassa had moved again, to Camp Street. The building survives in other use.

new_value: Ernie K-Doe's "Mother-in-Law" topped the national pop and rhythm and blues charts in May 1961. By the 1980s he was better known in New Orleans for his outlandish, free-associating radio shows on WWOZ. In 1995 Antoinette Fox, whom he later married, opened this lounge on North Claiborne Avenue, and it gave the self-styled Emperor of the Universe a stage and a late revival. After he died on July 5, 2001, Antoinette kept it going, with a dressed mannequin of her husband on display, through the 2005 flood and until her own death on Mardi Gras Day 2009. The lounge closed in 2010. Trumpeter Kermit Ruffins reopened it in 2014; in September 2026 he announced he was giving it up.

new_value: The city's Municipal Auditorium opened in 1930 beside Congo Square as an opera house, concert hall, arena and Carnival ballroom in one. Its history tracks segregation in New Orleans music: there were protests over balcony access for Marian Anderson's concert in 1940, Louis Jordan called from the stage for an integrated audience in 1948, and an integrated event was held in 1953. Louis Armstrong, Mahalia Jackson, Fats Domino and Elvis Presley all played here. Ernie K-Doe battled James Brown in 1962, jazz festivals in 1968 and 1969 led to the first Jazz and Heritage Festival in 1970, and George Clinton premiered the Mothership in 1976. Flooded in 2005, it has stood vacant since; repairs began in 2025.
reason: A Closer Walk does not call the 1953 event the first integrated one; the city confirms the building has been closed since Katrina and that Phase I repairs started in 2025.

new_value: The Ivanhoe was a club at 601 Bourbon Street. Around 1967 Art Neville's band, the Neville Sound, was pared down to become its house group: Neville on organ, Leo Nocentelli on guitar, George Porter Jr. on bass and Joseph "Zigaboo" Modeliste on drums. Playing six nights a week, the four tightened into a rhythm section and worked out long, spare instrumental grooves that won a local following. Allen Toussaint made them his studio band, and in 1969, renamed the Meters, they put their first four singles on the Hot 100, built from material developed at the Ivanhoe. The Radiators later traced their start to a 1971 jam session here. The building is now a different bar.

new_value: The New Orleans Jazz Club, founded in 1948, opened a jazz museum at 1017 Dumaine Street in 1961. It moved to the Royal Sonesta Hotel in 1969 and to Conti Street in 1973, then ran into money trouble and went into storage. On September 15, 1977, the whole collection was given to the Louisiana State Museum, which was renovating the Old U.S. Mint on Esplanade Avenue. The Mint opened to the public in 1981, and the jazz exhibit opened there in October 1983, the start year used here. The holdings include Louis Armstrong's first cornet, about 4,000 78 rpm records and some 12,000 photographs. The building also has a performance hall on its third floor.

new_value: Charles "Buddy" Bolden moved into this shotgun double on First Street in Central City in 1887, when he was ten, and lived here until 1906. These were the years in which he became the cornetist whom later players such as King Oliver and Louis Armstrong looked back to: his band came together around 1895, the start year used here, and worked Baptist church phrasing and dance hall blues into improvised dance music. After psychotic episodes and several arrests he was committed to the state hospital at Jackson in 1907 and died there in 1931. The house was landmarked in 1978. A church that bought it in 2008 was cited for neglect; PJ Morton's foundation has repaired it since 2023.
reason: The neglect citations are confirmed (Syncopated Times: 2011 and 2014; PRC: several more), but ownership changed in 2023 and the house was repaired in 2024.
